subject.title: Alameda — Measure N (Charter Amendment - Leases and Sales of Real Property Measure)

text: Proposed City Charter Amendment Ballot Measure Shall the measure amending Section 3-10 of the City Charter to change sales or leases of City real property exceeding one year to be approved by resolution rather than by ordinance and to reduce the City Council approval threshold from supermajority (four affirmative votes) to simple majority three affirmative votes) for leases of City real property not exceeding ten years be adopted?

This Measure was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Alameda acting upon the recommendations of an ad-hoc Charter Review Subcommittee. If approved by voters, this Measure would amend the Alameda City Charter to 1) allow the City Council to approve acquisitions, transfers (including sales), or leases of City-owned real property by resolution rather than by ordinance, and 2) allow the City Council to approve leases of City-owned real property for terms of less than 10 years by majority rather than supermajority vote.
Currently, under the City of Alameda City Charter, all acts of the Council providing for the acquisition, transfer/sale, or lease of City-owned real property for a term longer than one year must be adopted by ordinance. Ordinances must be adopted at two separate Council meetings and require a 30-day waiting period after final adoption before they take effect. By contrast, resolutions may be adopted at a single meeting and take effect immediately upon adoption by Council. Accordingly, if approved by voters, this Charter amendment would shorten by approximately 45 days the timeline for Council approvals of acquisition, transfer/sale, or lease of City-owned real property.
Additionally, under the current version of the City Charter, all acts of the Council providing for the acquisition, transfer/sale, or lease of City-owned real property for a term longer than one year must be approved by a Council supermajority (i.e., at least 4 out 5 Councilmembers voting “yes”). If approved by voters, this Charter amendment would reduce this requirement to a simple majority (i.e., at least 3 out of 5 Councilmembers voting “yes”) for leases with terms 10 years or less. However, leases with terms greater than 10 years will still need approval by a Council supermajority. Nothing in this Measure modifies Alameda City Charter Section 22-12, which requires (and will continue to require even if this Measure is adopted) voter approval for sales of City public parks.
A “Yes” vote is a vote to allow Council approval of acquisitions, transfers, or leases of City real property by resolution; and to allow Council approval of leases of less than 10 years by simple majority. A “No” vote is a vote to retain the requirement that Council approval of acquisitions, transfers, or leases of City real property must occur by ordinance, and that leases of more than one year but less than 10 years be approved by a Council supermajority. This Measure would take effect if approved by a majority of the voters who vote on the Measure.

Alameda’s future depends on our ability to make careful decisions and to act when good opportunities arise. Vote YES on this measure to modernize the City's outdated process for approving leases and property transactions. Today, even routine leases can require unnecessary procedural steps and, in some cases, a supermajority vote. These requirements can delay negotiations, discourage prospective tenants, and make Alameda less competitive with other communities. The problem is especially significant at Alameda Point, where successful redevelopment depends on attracting businesses, services, and organizations willing to invest in our community. This measure creates a more practical and balanced process. Leases of ten years or less could be approved by a majority of the City Council, allowing the City to respond more quickly to qualified tenants while preserving public review and accountability. Leases longer than ten years would continue to require four Council votes, maintaining an added safeguard for the City's most consequential long-term commitments.
The measure would allow the Council to approve leases and sales of City property by resolution rather than ordinance. That change eliminates an unnecessary second meeting while preserving public notice, open discussion, and a recorded vote by elected Councilmembers. It does not remove public oversight or permit staff to make these decisions behind closed doors. Every proposed transaction would remain subject to a public agenda, Council deliberation, and approval on its merits.
A more efficient process will help Alameda fill vacant properties, generate revenue, support local jobs, and accelerate the transformation of Alameda Point into a thriving mixed-use community. It will also strengthen the City's reputation as a responsible and responsive partner for businesses and nonprofit organizations.
This is a sensible reform that preserves accountability while removing delays that serve little practical purpose. Vote YES to help Alameda act efficiently, attract responsible investment, and move important community projects forward.

helps ensure that City Council doesn't proceed so fast as to only accommodate developers or commercial tenants; the requirement

ensures that Council accounts for the People's needs.
The examples below illustrate that, even with the current 4-vote requirement

, City Council approved many sales and leases for new private projects that included public amenities for the enjoyment of our residents -- especially at Alameda Point, where much city-owned property is located:
Bayport: a well-planned single-family home neighborhood built around an elementary school, a 4-acre park, and four smaller “pocket parks”.
Alameda Landing: a large commercial-residential project that included the waterfront Bohol Circle Immigrant Park.
"Site A": an 800 high-density units residential project involving the creation of the beautiful Seaplane Lagoon waterfront park.
The Alameda Food Bank: a modern, well-designed, family-friendly service (https://archive.ph/r37ZK).
Natel: a climate technology company leasing space along hangar row.

Pyka: an autonomous electric aircraft tenant with science projects for youths.
The above shows the current 4-vote requirement

does not hold up progress.
Thus, there is no compelling reason to weaken
longstanding protections offered by the current

4-vote requirement.
Keep the 4-vote requirement

: it is an important tool that keeps in check anyone eyeing Alameda properties: giving up Alameda’s valuable assets requires a consensus of at least all-but-one of the council members.
The 4-vote requirement was an issue in a 2023 matter involving a Marina Village live animal-testing (“neuralink lab monkeys” : https://archive.isim3bdX) business seeking to expand at Alameda Point, which was rejected in a Council vote that

text:
The opposition blurs the measure’s most important limits. This measure does not reduce the four-vote requirement for selling City property, nor does it reduce the requirement for leases longer than ten years. Those specific decisions will still require four affirmative Council votes.
The voting-threshold change applies only to leases of ten years or less, allowing the same three-vote majority normally used for Council decisions. Every such lease will still appear on a public agenda, receive public comment and Council debate, and require a recorded vote. A resolution removes a duplicative second reading and 30-day delay; it does not remove public oversight.
The large developments cited by opponents—Bayport, Alameda Landing, and Site A—do not explain why a shorter lease should require a supermajority. Major sales and long-term leases would still require four affirmative votes. The Science Corporation example also does not prove the opposition’s point. The Council ultimately voted 4-1 not to proceed, and Alameda later prohibited animal testing on City-owned property. This measure does not repeal that protection. Alameda’s existing rule is unusually restrictive. In a City survey of 28 nearby jurisdictions, all but Oakland used majority approval for leases and sales, and three-quarters used resolutions rather than ordinances.
This is a limited reform: majority rule for shorter leases, continued supermajority protection for sales and longer commitments, and full public review.
Vote YES.
